title: Philosophy of science
examples: How is a belief proven to be scientific?
What is the difference between science and pseudoscience?
Can we ever prove a theory is absolutely true?

explain.say: Today we are looking at what makes a claim scientific. We will explore ideas from the philosophy of science. Think about what separates real science from other kinds of thinking.
One key idea is falsifiability. This means a claim must be able to be proven false. If you cannot imagine how to prove it wrong, it might not be science.
Karl Popper was a philosopher who developed this idea. He argued that a theory must risk being proven wrong. This is central to his view of scientific progress.
A good example of falsifiability is gravity. If all objects fell up, the theory would be falsified. We test it by dropping objects.
In everyday life, consider astrology. Some claims sound predictive, but they are often too vague to be proven wrong. This makes them scientifically questionable.
A common mistake is assuming that because science is complex, it cannot be tested. Remember, science requires specific, risky predictions to be truly scientific.

faq.q: If a theory has been tested many times, is it proven true?
faq.a: No, science never proves anything absolutely true. It only shows that the theory has survived rigorous testing so far. You might ask, 'Does repeated testing prove truth?' or 'Is confirmation enough for science?'
asks: Does testing prove a theory correct?

faq.q: What is the difference between a hypothesis and a theory?
faq.a: A hypothesis is a testable, educated guess. A theory is a broad explanation supported by many confirmed hypotheses and evidence. You could also ask, 'What is the hierarchy of scientific ideas?'
asks: How does a hypothesis become a theory?

faq.q: Does every scientific statement have to be falsifiable?
faq.a: Yes, according to Popper's view, if a statement cannot, in principle, be proven wrong, it falls outside the realm of science. Another way to ask this is, 'Must science be refutable?'
asks: Can science talk about things that can't be tested?

faq.q: Is falsifiability the same as being testable?
faq.a: They are closely related, but falsifiability is stronger. It means there must be a specific, conceivable experiment that could prove it wrong. You might ask, 'Is testable the same as falsifiable?'
asks: What is the difference between the two terms?

faq.q: How does pseudoscience differ from real science?
faq.a: Pseudoscience often relies on accepting claims that cannot be tested or falsified by the scientific method. It resists being proven wrong. You could ask, 'What is the boundary between science and fake science?'
asks: What rules does science follow that fake science ignores?

facts: Falsifiability suggests a theory must make predictions that can be tested.
Karl Popper proposed falsifiability as a criterion for science.
A scientific claim must, in principle, be capable of being proven false.
Science progresses by eliminating incorrect theories.

quiz.say: Which criterion suggests a claim must be able to be proven wrong?
quiz.show: Falsifiability: Must be testable to be false

options.show: The claim must be accepted by most experts.
options.say: The claim must be accepted by most experts.

options.show: The claim must be based on ancient texts.
options.say: The claim must be based on ancient texts.

options.show: The claim must make predictions that can be tested.
options.say: The claim must make predictions that can be tested.

options.show: The claim must be very complicated.
options.say: The claim must be very complicated.

quiz.why: This is correct because falsifiability, as argued by Popper, requires a potential test that could disprove the idea.

wrong.0: Popular agreement does not make a claim scientific.
wrong.1: Scientific knowledge relies on empirical evidence, not just old writings.
wrong.3: Complexity is not the defining feature; testability is.

quiz.say: If a theory explains everything, what might be wrong with it?

options.show: It must be too simple to be true.
options.say: It must be too simple to be true.

options.show: It must be accepted by all people.
options.say: It must be accepted by all people.

options.show: It must be proven using only logic.
options.say: It must be proven using only logic.

quiz.why: A theory that explains every single outcome has no risk, and therefore, no predictive power to be tested.

wrong.0: Simplicity is not the requirement; testability is.
wrong.1: Scientific theories are debated, not universally accepted.
wrong.2: Science requires testing against the physical world, not just pure logic.

quiz.say: Which statement best describes the scientific approach?

options.show: It requires absolute proof before any claim is made.
options.say: It requires absolute proof before any claim is made.

options.show: It proposes testable hypotheses that risk being proven wrong.
options.say: It proposes testable hypotheses that risk being proven wrong.

options.show: It only accepts ideas that are simple to understand.
options.say: It only accepts ideas that are simple to understand.

options.show: It relies only on established facts from the past.
options.say: It relies only on established facts from the past.

quiz.why: This captures the entire cycle: proposing an idea, testing it, and being ready to change the idea if the test fails.

wrong.0: The scientific method is built on probabilities and potential disproof, not absolute proof.
wrong.2: Science deals with complexity, provided it is testable.
wrong.3: Science must make predictions about the future, not just repeat the past.
